item.title: Federal appeals court again denies Trump admin request to block 20,000 California ballots
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
An open voting machine is seen at Arroyo Seco regional branch library on Oct. 27 in Los Angeles. (Ronaldo Bolaños / Los Angeles Times) A federal appeals court for the second time Friday denied a Trump administration request to block 20,000 ballots from California voters the administration alleges may be noncitizens — ruling that the administration had failed to show that “such extraordinary relief, during an ongoing election, is clearly required by law.” The three-judge panel of the U.S. 9th Circuit Court of Appeals — composed of two appointees of President Trump and one of President Biden — ruled 2-1 that the U.S. Constitution gives the state and Congress the power to decide how elections are run, and that allowing the Trump administration to “misuse” federal statutes to “prescribe” how California must process ballots would “override the plain and manifest dictates of the Constitution itself.” “Because Congress has not exercised the specific power granted to it under the Elections Clause to override California’s established laws for challenging ballots or removing ineligible voters, the State Legislature’s statutory scheme remains the only method to do so,” the judges found. The panel’s majority — comprised of Trump appointee Mark J. Bennett and Biden appointee Gabriel P. Sanchez — wrote that “if the United States believes different procedures are necessary for vote-by-mail ballots, we believe it should take that suggestion to Congress, not the courts.” They also wrote that separate federal law proscribes sweeping changes to voter lists 90 days prior to an election, especially given questions about the reliability of the Trump administration’s list of purported noncitizens. “The suspect reliability of these lists found by the district court reflects the concern Congress sought to mitigate with the 90-day quiet period,” they wrote. Judge Patrick J. Bumatay, the other Trump appointee on the panel, dissented — arguing that his colleagues erred in denying a basic request by the Trump administration to ensure only citizens are voting. “The federal government proposes a modest remedy — stopping California from mixing the ballots of citizens and suspected noncitizens,” Bumatay wrote. “This solution would not cancel any vote but would allow time to verify the eligibility of suspected noncitizens. The district court, and now our court, denies this reasonable request.” This article will be updated. Read more: California, feds continue election war after courts rebuke challenge to 20,000 ballots Read more: Your last-minute guide to in-person voting for California's general election Get the L.A. Times California Politics newsletter. Deeply reported insights into legislation, politics and policy from Sacramento, Washington and beyond, in your inbox twice per week. This story originally appeared in Los Angeles Times . This article originally appeared on LA Times at https://www.yahoo.com/news/politics/articles/9th-circuit-again-denies-trump-191628973.html

item.title: 'It could be quite a brutal evening': GOP braces for some once-unthinkable losses
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
Republicans are bracing for a brutal election night, convinced they're set to face some previously unthinkable losses in deep-red Trump territory as key battleground races hang on a knife's edge . House Republicans are privately discussing not just if they'll lose their majority, but by how many seats. Imperiled GOP incumbents in once safe districts have been begging party leaders for more money in the final few days to stem the bleeding, according to six people involved in internal conversations, granted anonymity to discuss them. Senate Republicans have found new cause to worry about contests in Ohio, Kansas and other red states. "It could be quite a brutal evening," said one senior Republican involved in the private conversations, who like others in this article was granted anonymity to speak candidly. "Once the dominoes start falling it becomes hard to stop them." Some Republican incumbents made an eyebrow-raising emergency decision. They stopped doing their own polling weeks ago as they tried to save every dollar for swaying voters as they begged for the GOP cavalry to arrive from President Donald Trump's political operation to the National Republican Congressional Committee, according to three of the people. One Republican strategist working on midterm races simply responded to a question about the environment with a video of a dumpster on fire that was being swept away by flood waters. Top GOP officials and lawmakers have long known the political landscape would be bad, amid voter anger over the cost of living and aspects of Trump's policy agenda. But they're facing a worse position than they expected earlier this year, with less than one week until Election Day. Republicans for weeks have worried that young men who'd voted for Trump, including white and Hispanic working class voters, will stay home amid disillusionment with high costs and the Iran war. That alone could allow Democrats to overperform in some areas after they hemorrhaged support among that voting bloc in 2024. At a Kwik Trip in Eau Claire, Wisconsin, this week in the hotly-contested 3rd District, Isaiah Romero was filling up his silver Ram truck. The 20-year-old said he cast his ballot for Trump in his first ever presidential election two years ago. His verdict on high fuel prices? "I think they're bull," he said as he looked over to the $6.39 per gallon diesel and $4.29 gas at the pump. Is he voting this time? "No," Romero responded, adding: "I didn't vote for this." New fires have been popping up across the map just as soon as top GOP officials put out others. Trump canceled in-person rallies in deep-red Kansas and Iowa set for this weekend to instead hold a series of tele-rallies for GOP candidates in the final stretch. "Any Democrats telling you they aren't winning the Senate [besides] a couple of seats are sandbagging expectations," the senior Republican said. In Ohio, the race between GOP Sen. Jon Husted and former Democratic Sen. Sherrod Brown is still incredibly close in private and public polling. But Republicans have watched with horror as GOP governor nominee "Vivek's [Ramaswamy's] numbers have gone off a cliff" in the last few days after he ran an ad featuring Democrat Amy Acton's estranged mother saying her daughter is a liar, according to the senior Republican and two others who saw the internal polling. Acton's stepfather was charged with raping her when she was 12. The headwinds across all of Ohio are deeply problematic for Republicans. They now believe embattled Rep. Max Miller (R-Ohio) — who is facing child and domestic abuse allegations that he denies — will lose in a seat Trump won by double digits. South Carolina has become another unexpectedly nailbiting race for Republicans, where political newcomer Sen. Darline Graham is facing a well-funded Democratic challenger. But GOP operatives and officials are feeling somewhat better after outside groups injected cash into the race earlier this month and Trump announced another rally in the state to energize Republicans' base. "It's a lot closer than I think we would ever want, but I think she's going to pull it out," said Jeff Davis, chair of the Greenville County Republican Party. But in one of the most dire signs, once-unimaginable GOP worries have started to creep about deep-red Louisiana — where Trump announced this week he will hold an election-eve tele-rally for Senate nominee Julia Letlow. Speaker Mike Johnson, who is close with Letlow, will join as Republicans have grown wary about a surge of Black voters and other Democratic-leaning voters in early voting across the South. Senior Republicans believe Letlow will win, but they fear it will be by single digits if nothing changes. "The cakewalk turned into a knife fight," said one Louisiana Republican who has talked with Letlow recently. "If Democrat turnout surges on Election Day, it'll be a long night in Monroe," the person added, and they expect Letlow to win by just 6 points in a state Trump won by 22 points two years ago. In another painful development for Republicans in Louisiana, GOP groups have even started an eye-popping spending war in a safe red gerrymandered seat — where a bitter Republican-on-Republican primary is unfolding between state Sen. Blake Miguez, who was formerly endorsed by Trump , and state Sen. Rick Edmonds, Johnson's former pastor. Club for Growth poured another $220,000 into the race Thursday. Republicans fear the messy race is poised for a December runoff. "POLITICO's sad little rolodex of loser strategists have no idea what they're talking about, and if they really believe what they're saying they should come out of the shadows and put a name to their brain-dead comments," said RNC spokesperson Natalie Baldassarre. "While Republicans have focused on real solutions to improve costs of living and make our nation safer, Democrats have nominated a gang of radicals who want to raise taxes, force everyone on government healthcare, and release criminals onto the streets," said Joanna Rodriguez, spokesperson for the National Republican Senatorial Committee. On the House side, Republicans are bracing for a brutal night. But they've long been spending in some redder GOP districts to forestall a true disaster. Mike Marinella, a spokesperson for the NRCC, said that the committee worked in partnership with the campaigns and the RNC to launch coordinated advertising early in GOP-held districts not initially rated as competitive, including those represented by Reps. Jeff Hurd (Colo.), Bill Huizenga (Mich.), Rob Wittman (Va.), Mike Turner (Ohio), and Monica De La Cruz (Texas). The NRCC began airing coordinated ads in early August, more than a month before the DCCC. The NRCC also conducted polling in more than 100 districts, an eye-popping number, as they worked to see how far the fires had spread into red terrain and make sure they were moving resources where they were needed. Republicans still think they can unseat Rep. Marie Gluesenkamp Perez (D-Wash.) and Gabe Vasquez (D-N.M.), while flipping retiring Rep. Jared Golden's (D-Maine) seat. But privately, Republicans believe North Carolina's open 11th District is close to gone, as are several other deep-red seats Trump won by double digits, according to four people with knowledge of the situation. And they're still not confident they'll beat Rep. Don Davis (D-N.C.) in a seat the GOP thought would be an easy flip when they redrew it early this year. It's become the most expensive House race in history. The Republican in Kentucky's 6th district, where Trump won by 15 points in 2024, is barely hanging on, according to the four people. Even in the South Texas districts the GOP redrew in their favor, Republicans reached the point days ago where no amount of new money is going to change the upcoming catastrophe, said one Republican official involved in conversations about those races. Johnson traveled to Minnesota on Thursday to headline a fundraiser for GOP Rep. Brad Finstad, who Republicans are scrambling to shore up in a +12 Trump district. Finstad told POLITICO in an interview this week that he had warned senior Republicans for weeks about Democratic groups pouring money into the race in his southern Minnesota district. "We raised that with anybody and everybody that would want to hear it," Finstad said. "From a global perspective, people were like, 'Well, you won by 18, you're fine.' And, you know, those of us in Minnesota know that this district has always had kind of an independent streak to it." Senate Democrats, meanwhile, are upbeat at their prospects, but public and private polling across close to the entire battleground map is running within the margin of error — meaning those states could break either way. "I would rather be us than them. But if anyone tells you they know what's going to happen, they're full of shit," one senior Senate Democratic operative said. "Everything is close." And some Republicans are taking solace in the fact that at least it'll all soon be over. "I can see the light at the end of the tunnel," said a GOP strategist working on a campaign that is trending toward Democrats. "It might be a semi-truck, but at least I can see it." Andrew Howard, Erin Doherty and Alec Hernández contributed to this report. This article originally appeared on Politico at https://www.yahoo.com/news/politics/articles/could-quite-brutal-evening-gop-090000456.html

item.title: Netanyahu's party claims election was stolen as results show him losing majority
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
Tel Aviv — Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and his Likud party alleged Thursday that Israel's election earlier in the week was stolen by Arab-majority parties, helped by foreign funding that amounted to vote-buying, as final results showed Netanyahu's bloc has lost its majority in Israel's parliament, the Knesset. Israel's Arab-majority parties had their highest turnout ever in Tuesday's election, winning an unprecedented 19 of the Knesset's 120 seats. Their success is one of the main reasons Netanyahu's bloc lost its majority and can't now form a new government. The final election results show the far-right wing bloc's share of Knesset seats fell from 68 to 53. Israel's Arab minority, also called Palestinian citizens of Israel, makes up about 20% of the country's population. "Israel's elections have been stolen," Netanyahu's Likud party declared in a statement Thursday, claiming "an attack on democracy aimed at leading to a foreign takeover of the Knesset, the Islamization of Israel, and the overthrow of the right-wing government to cause a withdrawal and defeat of the IDF (Israeli military) on all fronts — first and foremost, Iran." The four parties that make up the main bloc opposing Netanyahu won 48 seats, so they would need some support from the Arab parties to try to form a coalition government, assuming none of the lawmakers currently aligned with Netanyahu's bloc defect. The heads of Israel's two biggest Arab parties, which collectively won 19 seats, have said they would be willing to help the main opposition bloc oust Netanyahu from power. Most of the Jewish-led parties that oppose Netanyahu vowed before the election not to rely on support from Arab parties to form a government, however, leaving a question mark over whether they might now be willing to cooperate to build a coalition to unseat the incumbent prime minister. "No basis to the claims regarding a systematic compromise" The Shin Bet, Israel's internal security agency, said it had opened an investigation into possible foreign influence in the election, but the scope of that investigation has not been made clear. "An investigation of this type is also focused and bounded, and does not cast aspersions or place blame on an entire sector that went out to vote democratically and legally," the agency said in a Thursday statement. The Acting Director-General of the Central Elections Committee, Din Livne, said in a letter to a committee member on Thursday that "there is no basis to the claims regarding a systematic compromise of the integrity of the elections." Israel media reports said one of the allegations the Shin Bet investigation would consider was whether Qatar had sent money to Arab parties in order to increase turnout among Arab Israeli voters. Qatar's foreign ministry has denied the accusation. "We categorically deny allegations that Qatar has interfered in Israeli elections or funded any activities intended to influence their outcome," ministry spokesperson Majid Al-Ansari said. "Qatar should not be used as a scapegoat for the political failures of certain Israeli politicians." "An improper influence operation?" While vote counting is now officially complete, the election results must still be certified and sent to President Issac Herzog before a new parliament can be sworn in and the process of forming a new government begins. Gadi Eisenkot, head of the centrist Yashar party and the top candidate to replace Netanyahu as prime minister, said he was worried that Netanyahu could be using the allegation of a stolen election to justify delaying or disqualifying the results. "Netanyahu, who has accustomed himself to dealing with reality through lies, consciousness engineering, and the spreading of chaos, is leading alongside his partners an improper influence operation on the Israeli public aimed at delaying the publication of the election results on time and creating fictitious delegitimization of the activity of the 26th Knesset," Eisenkot said Thursday in a social media post. Once the new Knesset is sworn in — even without a new government decided on — Eisenkot's bloc, along with the Arab parties, could begin passing laws given that they will control a majority in the parliament. Netanyahu, who President Trump endorsed enthusiastically , will remain in his post as a caretaker prime minister until a new government is formed. If the parties cannot negotiate to form a new coalition government, then the country would have to hold the election all over again, and Netanyahu would remain the prime minister in the interim. This article originally appeared on CBS News at https://www.cbsnews.com/news/israel-election-results-netanyahu-likud-claim-stolen-arab-parties/

item.title: Pentagon reportedly tells NATO allies to tone down rhetoric about Russia
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
By Antoni Slodkowski, Gram Slattery and Andrius Sytas Oct 30 (Reuters) - Pentagon officials have in recent weeks asked several NATO countries to tone down their rhetoric regarding the threat posed by Russia, arguing that some statements by European leaders and officials have undermined continental security, four people familiar with the matter said. Among the nations that have received ‌messages urging them to keep public statements in check are Lithuania, Latvia and Estonia, said the people, who spoke on condition of anonymity. It was not clear if the messages, ‌which were delivered in bilateral meetings, were conveyed to other European governments. The US requests come as the Trump administration restarts an effort to press for a negotiated end to the full-scale war in Ukraine, now well into its fifth year. The ​latest push has blended incentives for Russia - including sanctions relief - with pressure on Ukraine to halt its attacks on Russian energy infrastructure. Asked for comment, a Pentagon official said: "Private conversations among allies are just that, so we will not comment on these allegations." Among the comments that have drawn US officials' attention are suggestions by European leaders that Russia is cornered and resorting to increasingly desperate measures as its invasion of Ukraine slows to a crawl, one of the people said. Pentagon policy chief Elbridge Colby, a key figure in an ongoing review of US troop levels in Europe, was one of the US officials delivering the message, the people said. ‌Reuters could not determine what other officials were involved. None of the people, ⁠who include three European officials and a US official, suggested the advice was communicated in a confrontational manner. EUROPE SHOULD AVOID "POKING" RUSSIA The US messages reflect a debate within NATO regarding how to publicly address the threat of an increasingly assertive Russia. Some Western officials have argued that emphasizing the threat posed by Moscow could play ⁠into the hands of the Kremlin, which they say seeks to sow fear and undermine support for Ukraine. Others argue European governments must be transparent to show their electorates that sacrifice and resources are needed to keep Moscow at bay. That is especially true as Russia appears to accelerate a covert campaign of sabotage throughout the continent. Russia has denied that it is pursuing such a campaign. One of the people familiar told Reuters that Colby told a ​Baltic ​official recently that there should be no "poking" directed at the Russians. The person said Colby pointed to Europeans publicly suggesting ​that Russia was "cornered like a rat" as an example of unhelpful rhetoric. It was ‌not clear what specific statement Colby was referring to. However, Estonian Prime Minister Kristen Michal referred to Putin as a "rat in a corner" in late September, suggesting the Russian leader was resorting to sabotage efforts in Europe as Russia had become increasingly bogged down in Ukraine. "We are helping you. The Americans are there," said a separate European official, describing the Pentagon's recent private messaging. "Just don't be loud. Don't make noise." In a separate recent meeting, the Pentagon urged an Estonian delegation to be "measured" in its communications, according to a person briefed on the encounter, though the person did not say Pentagon officials complained about any specific statement. The defense ministries of Lithuania, Latvia and Estonia did not respond to requests for comment, while NATO declined to comment. MOSCOW TESTS EUROPE'S RESOLVE One of the European officials said that the Pentagon's advice, ‌while cordial, was baffling, given that intelligence services in the Baltic states have in recent months consistently played down ​the probability of Russia testing NATO's mutual defense provisions. Other NATO intelligence services, by contrast, have publicly warned that Russia could ​dramatically ramp up its sabotage campaign in the near future. The Pentagon messages to NATO officials ​come at a fraught time for European security. Moscow has recently intensified its campaign of deniable attacks on NATO countries, Western intelligence officials have said. On Wednesday, German prosecutors ‌said two Belarusians were arrested for allegedly planning to set fire to a ​building or critical infrastructure facility in the Nuremberg ​area. In September, the German government blamed Russia for an attempted drone attack at Leipzig/Halle Airport, allegations Moscow has denied. At the same time, US officials have been discussing potential business deals with Russia as part of the Trump administration's push for peace in Ukraine. Those efforts have drawn mixed reactions from European officials, many of whom are pushing for the Kremlin's continued ​economic isolation. Pentagon planners, meanwhile, are reviewing Washington's force posture in Europe, a ‌process that could see a sharp drawdown in America's troop presence on the continent. US officials have said European NATO members need to assume more responsibility for their own defense, ​particularly as the US focuses on threats in the Middle East, Latin America and East Asia. (Reporting by Antoni Slodkowski in New York, Gram Slattery in Washington and Andrius ​Sytas in Vilnius; Additional reporting by Phil Stewart in Washington; Editing by Don Durfee and Alistair Bell) This article originally appeared on Reuters at https://www.yahoo.com/news/articles/exclusive-pentagon-tells-europeans-cool-050400616.html

item.title: U.S. scraps G20 group photo after European diplomats refuse to pose with Russia's Lavrov
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
ATLANTA (AP) — The top diplomats from the Group of 20 largest world economies opened two days of meetings in Atlanta on Friday after European objections to Russia’s participation forced the U.S. to cancel a photo of the foreign ministers, underscoring deep rifts among the group over global crises . Secretary of State Marco Rubio pulled the plug on the traditional group photo after several European officials threatened to boycott or walk out of the snapshot that usually helps kick off such diplomatic gatherings. But he still opened the talks, which otherwise went ahead as planned, with an appeal for unity on the issues that threaten international security and trade. “We are in a critical moment — I would call it a moment of choosing, and I would say not just for my country, the United States of America, but frankly, for the world," Rubio told his colleagues. “We are facing a series of interconnected economic and geopolitical crises,” he added, pointing to disruptions to global energy and food supplies, trade and freedom of navigation. Many are posing “severe threats to essential foundations of the global economic order.” Yet there was no sign that the G20 diplomats could come to consensus on many of the most contentious issues they face. Among them are the Russia-Ukraine conflict, the U.S.-Israeli war against Iran , U.S. tariffs and Chinese machinations in the South China Sea . All have contributed to spikes in the global cost of fuel as well as uncertainty about trade. Russia's presence at G20 gathering roils European allies Concerns about any prospects for the talks escalated when the Europeans balked at being photographed with Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov. Rubio decided to scrap the picture because he thought the controversy would be a distraction, according to two U.S. officials, who spoke on condition of anonymity due to the sensitivity of the matter. Some G20 countries had already expressed concern that the U.S. invited Russia during its heightened attacks on Ukraine, especially after Trump pushed ties with Ukraine to new lows by waiving fresh sanctions on Moscow and temporarily limiting logistical and intelligence assistance. The British foreign office said in a statement that the United Kingdom “has a longstanding policy not to have direct, bilateral engagement with Russian ministers since the invasion of Ukraine and we are not about to change that.” Polish Deputy Prime Minister and Foreign Minister Radosław Sikorski said the cancellation of the group photo was “the right decision” by the U.S., telling media in Atlanta that “I am not the only one who does not want to be photographed with Lavrov.” German Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul said “there is no normality with Russia” but “we must exchange the controversies at the table here,” the German news agency dpa reported. He added that “we also must not send falsely optimistic signals.” Lavrov has traveled only infrequently to NATO member states since Russia invaded Ukraine in February 2022 and resulting severe sanctions were imposed on Moscow. His presence in Atlanta could cause domestic political problems for Trump just days before the U.S. congressional midterm elections as well as roil the G20, according to Ian Kelly, a U.S. ambassador to Georgia during Trump’s first term. “It seems politically boneheaded to invite him,” said Kelly, who now teaches international relations and diplomacy at Northwestern University outside Chicago. The meeting in Atlanta is meant to set the stage for a G20 leaders’ summit hosted by President Donald Trump at his Miami golf club in December. It is unclear if Russian President Vladimir Putin will accept Trump’s invitation to that gathering. G20 member South Africa was not invited Ukraine, which is not a G20 member but was invited to attend previous such meetings, was not invited this year as U.S. officials said they made a conscious choice to include only formal members of the group. But missing from the invite list was South Africa, a G20 founding member and the only African country in the group. South Africa is embroiled in several bitter disputes with the Trump administration, and when it chaired the G20 last year, top U.S. officials, including Trump and Rubio, shunned the meetings it hosted. “We have consistently maintained that our nonparticipation is not voluntary,” said Phindile Kunene, spokesperson for South African Foreign Minister Ronald Lamola. Kunene welcomed support from other G20 members that had expressed reservations about the exclusion and said South Africa was ready to participate “on an equal footing with other members” when Britain takes over the presidency next year. The Iran war hangs over the G20 event The U.S. has said a top priority for the meeting is resolving differences over issues related to freedom of navigation, particularly in the Strait of Hormuz , the Red Sea, the Black Sea and the South China Sea. The topic will include discussions on Iran, Russia-Ukraine and China and its smaller neighbors. But hanging over the meeting is the prospect of new U.S. military intervention in Iran, which has put the region, including G20 member Saudi Arabia, on edge. The Associated Press has reported that U.S. officials have told several Middle East countries and regional allies to be prepared for potential renewed military strikes against Iran after Tuesday’s midterm elections and the possibility that Iran will retaliate against them. ___ Associated Press writers Michelle Gumede in Johannesburg, South Africa, Claudia Ciobanu in Warsaw, Poland, Geir Moulson in Berlin, Jill Lawless in London and Farnoush Amiri in New York contributed. item.title: 'I'm deeply hurt': Christa Pike speaks after surviving lethal injection
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
Christa Pike is speaking out publicly for the first time since she survived an execution attempt by the state of Tennessee on Sept. 30. "There hasn't been a moment since that night when I haven't been in pain," Pike said in her first public statement since the execution attempt, which her legal team shared Friday. "My body hurts. My arms hurt. My hands hurt. My throat hurts. I still struggle to speak. And the pain isn't just physical. There is pain in my mind and in my soul." Pike, 50, was sentenced to death in 1996 for the murder of her classmate, Colleen Slemmer, and spent 30 years on death row. Two doses of the lethal injection drug pentobarbital failed to kill her during the state's execution attempt last month. She was taken to the hospital, where she received lifesaving care. Slemmer's mother, May Martinez , described the situation as a "mess" and said she was left without justice. “I’m deeply hurt by the incompetence that has put so many people in this terrible position,” Pike said. "I continue to think about my victim's family and the terrible pain and loss they have endured." Pike's legal team described the outcome as "unprecedented" and said it has raised questions about what happens next in her case. "I don't know why I survived that night," Pike added. "I don't know what comes next. Some days, finding hope is harder than others. For now, I am trying to heal, one day at a time. And I am holding on to the love and kindness of so many people who have reminded me that I am not alone." Pike's survival has brought intense scrutiny to Tennessee's execution procedures. Gov. Bill Lee suspended the one remaining execution scheduled for this year, and the state's top prison official, Correction Commissioner Frank Strada, is stepping down at the end of October. Pike's lawyers said the resignation was "justified, but it does nothing to help Christa now. They said the botched execution "reflects a systemic failure that goes far beyond any one person," they said in a statement issued earlier this month, according to ABC News . Pike has been held at the Debra K. Johnson Rehabilitation Center since Oct. 10, where she has been behind bars for more than 30 years. She continues to receive medical care in the prison's infirmary. "I am recovering, and I know that I am getting stronger," her statement read. "But healing is not the same as being okay." What was Christa Pike's condition after the botched execution? When Pike arrived at the hospital, her arms were "swollen, burned and blistered," her lawyers wrote in a legal filing on Oct. 2. Her lawyers believe the IV lines were placed incorrectly or her veins burst, so that some or all of the drug went into the tissue of her arms instead of her bloodstream. Her condition was so severe in the following days, after the execution attempt, that it was believed that she may be brain-dead and could be removed from life support the following day, Randy Spivey, one of her attorneys, said during a press conference on Oct. 7. "On Tuesday, to the shock of everyone … Christa woke up and began talking," he said. Spivey added that Pike is feeling "angry and confused" after waking up in the hospital and is still dealing with major physical problems from the failed execution, including a blood clot, pneumonia and swelling that has left her unable to use both of her arms. "Her recovery is medically unprecedented. Her prognosis remains unclear but, at a minimum, we expect a long recovery," her legal team wrote in a court filing on Oct. 6. Dr. Joel Zivot, a medical expert who has consulted with Pike's legal team, told the Associated Press that the latest update "bodes well for a good recovery," but said that the full picture of her long-term health will not be clear for some time. "She has recovered to a certain degree that she's able to be off a ventilator and able to speak, but in no way would I announce her free of further serious risk," he said. "There's still a lot of bad things that can happen here." Pike, pictured in 2007, is conscious and speaking in the hospital, according to her legal team. via REUTERS / REUTERS Deborah Denno, a criminologist and professor at Fordham Law School, told the BBC that she was "absolutely astonished" that Pike was conscious and speaking. "They did everything they were supposed to do as part of the execution process, and it simply didn't work," she said. "This has never happened before." Dr. Zivot told the BBC that her survival was "unusual," adding, "Most people who get lethal injection die from it. In fact, pretty well everyone, except Christa." Seattle University Law Professor Michael Russo told the Associated Press, "There's nobody else in the history of the death penalty in this country who has gone through what she's been through." The incident with Pike comes a handful of months after the botched attempt to execute Tony Carruthers . In May, Tennessee stopped the execution of Carruthers after staff placed an IV into his right arm, but were unable to insert a secondary IV line. What happens next? All executions in Tennessee are paused for now. Pike's lawyers have called for her sentence to be commuted. State officials have not said whether they will try to execute Pike again, and Gov. Lee has not indicated that he plans to intervene in Pike's case. Lee had denied Pike's clemency before the execution attempt. "I think at the very least the governor should commute Ms. Pike's death sentence to a life sentence," attorney Stephen Ferrell told CNN's State of the Union earlier this month. "We don't know what her physical state will be, but it is clear that she has endured a torturous attempt at executing her." Dr. Zivot said it remains unclear how much pentobarbital entered Pike's system, how much remained in her blood after the injection and what effects she could still experience as she recovers. "I would not, in any way, say at this point that all the big risks are behind her," he said. Professor Russo doubted whether the Supreme Court would stop the state from trying again on double jeopardy grounds — the constitutional protection against being tried or punished twice for the same offense — should it decide to do so. He said, "I think what this Supreme Court would say is, her sentence was to die — to be executed — not to suffer an attempt at execution." "We're in uncharted territory," Robin Maher, executive director of the nonprofit Death Penalty Information Center, told USA Today . "The U.S. Supreme Court has not decided whether a second execution attempt would violate the Constitution since 1947. These are questions that have never needed to be asked before, and no one knows the answers." item.title: Stocks plunge on the final trading day of October as AI reckoning grips Wall Street
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
US stocks plunged in the final trading day of the month as earnings from Amazon ( AMZN ) and Alphabet ( GOOG , GOOGL ) this week rekindled concerns about the amount of money Big Tech is spending on its AI ambitions. The Nasdaq Composite ( ^IXIC ) tumbled 2.8% as a tech-fueled sell-off intensified. The Dow Jones Industrial Average ( ^DJI ) fell 1.2%, or over 650 points, while the S&P 500 ( ^GSPC ) dropped 2%. For the month, the Dow gained 1.5%, while the Nasdaq and S&P 500 gave up gains, falling 5.2% and 1.2%, respectively. October marked the worst month for the Nasdaq since March 2025. Stocks fell for the second day in a row after Amazon and Alphabet posted rare earnings misses , renewing concerns about the sustainability of the AI boom. Amazon shares fell 2%, while Alphabet continued to erase market value after its stock suffered its worst day in over 20 years. Intel ( INTC ) also suffered a brutal reaction to its earnings report, dropping 29% in premarket trading after the company's Q4 outlook came up short. One bright spot in the market was ExxonMobil ( XOM ) and Chevron ( CVX ), whose stocks briefly touched record highs after the oil majors reported that their earnings were boosted as refining margins widened amid the war in the Middle East. Pharmaceutical company AstraZeneca ( AZN ) also reported an earnings beat before the opening bell. While earnings remain in focus, oil prices rebounded higher, putting additional pressure on markets. Brent crude futures ( BZ=F ) rose to $112 per barrel, while WTI crude ( CL=F ) reached $104 per barrel. Bitcoin ( BTC-USD ) prices tumbled more than 2% as crypto assets were rattled following a $6.3 billion hack on cryptocurrency exchange Binance, marking the largest heist of its kind in history. item.title: ICE agent indicted on aggravated assault charge for allegedly hitting man with car
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
HOUSTON (AP) — A U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement officer accused of intentionally ramming his car into a Mexican construction worker in Houston was indicted by a grand jury Friday on a charge of aggravated assault with a deadly weapon, prosecutors said. The officer, Mario Alberto Morales, was driving an unmarked SUV on Oct. 10 when he struck and ran over Miguel Parra Hernandez, 48, who was running away during a pursuit through a parking lot, according to the Harris County District Attorney’s Office. Parra Hernandez broke his leg and remains in federal custody at a rehabilitation facility, said District Attorney Sean Teare, who announced the indictment at a news conference that included body camera video of the encounter and a recording of Morales calling 911. ICE has asserted that Parra Hernandez ran in front of the vehicle, an account that Teare said is contradicted by video. “The evidence we have in this case is as clear as any that I’ve ever prosecuted or investigated,” Teare said. Morales, 33, is one of just a few federal officers who have faced criminal charges over their actions on the job during President Donald Trump’s immigration crackdown , although other encounters have come under investigation , including a fatal shooting by an ICE officer this summer in Houston. Morales’ attorney, David Lindenmuth, said his client didn't commit a crime and he accused Teare of indicting Morales “for political gain.” Morales had worked as an ICE Enforcement and Removal Operations officer for a little more than a year, Lindenmuth said. “Mr. Morales is truly a good man, a former member of our military, that has given his entire life to public service either for his country or in or adjacent to law enforcement,” Lindenmuth told The Associated Press. “To have him charged for what was so clearly just an accident — the DA’s office, the DA himself, has invented a crime out of thin air.” Teare hinted at concerns over Morales' background but would not provide details. Morales, who is charged with a second-degree felony, was not in custody Friday and a warrant will be issued for his arrest, according to Teare. ICE asserted that local officials do not have the authority to investigate federal officers acting in the course of their duties. “Allegations that ICE struck Miguel Parra-Hernandez intentionally are RECKLESS and FALSE,” the agency said in a statement. The district attorney played Morales' body camera footage Teare has said video clearly contradicts the ICE account. Surveillance video shows a Jeep Cherokee speed over a median and drive toward Parra Hernandez as he runs away. During a news conference Friday, he played Morales' body camera footage, which shows him driving and talking about pursuing someone. The video shows Morales making a few sharp moves with the steering wheel before the SUV shakes. Morales stops the vehicle, then gets out and turns toward Parra Hernandez, who is several feet away. The video then shows Parra Hernandez on the ground and grabbing his leg, yelling in pain. Morales is heard saying, “He got hit with a car, bro.” It is not clear to whom he is talking. “I was coming in and I hit him with the car,” Morales says. Family says ICE was looking for a dead person during operation Parra Hernandez has lived in Harris County for more than 30 years and did not have a deportation order or criminal background, according to Teare. Other aspects of ICE's account have also been called into question . After Parra Hernandez was taken into custody, ICE released a photo of another man, Jose Mendoza-Cervantes, and said he was the target of the operation that day. ICE said he was seen entering a vehicle with Parra Hernandez. Family members of Parra Hernandez said they had never heard of him. FIEL, an immigrant rights group in Houston that has been working with the family, said Mendoza-Cervantes' daughter told them her father has been dead since 2017. Teare’s office has previously said its investigation has not found that Parra Hernandez and the man ICE identified as Mendoza-Cervantes were in a vehicle together, contrary to ICE’s statement. ICE has not responded to claims that the suspect they were looking for has been dead for years. Fatal summer Houston shooting also under investigation Teare has said the Department of Homeland Security, which oversees ICE, has not cooperated with his investigators and accused ICE of destroying evidence “either intentionally or through gross negligence.” He has said Morales left the scene before the vehicle could be impounded. In July, Teare said DHS also ignored his requests for information after an ICE officer fatally shot 52-year-old Lorenzo Salgado Araujo in his van. DHS has said Salgado Araujo had “weaponized his vehicle” before the shooting and that an officer fired in self-defense. Other passengers in the van have disputed that account . ___ Wilder reported from Austin, Texas. Brook reported from New Orleans. ___ Wilder is a corps member for The Associated Press/Report for America Statehouse News Initiative. Report for America is a nonprofit national service program that places journalists in local newsrooms to report on undercovered issues.
